notes:
Here are notes on Deuteronomy 4:1–24, based on the pages I could read. Each point gives its source page. I didn't find anything usable on vv. 4, 14 or 17–18 alone, or on Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Orthodox, bibleodyssey.org or prosperity/word of faith/hyper-grace views of this passage, so those are left out.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott says the whole chapter makes one appeal: serve the LORD. It rests on how God showed himself at Horeb. He also notes that life is put before possession. The penalty of the broken law is death. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Guzik says "that you may live" works on two levels. Spiritually, life depended on obeying. Physically too, since Israel was about to fight strong peoples, and he points to the defeat at Ai (Joshua 7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 2:** Guzik: don't *add* to God's word by treating human traditions as equal to it. Don't *take away* by bad teaching, explaining passages away, or calling biblical writers unreliable. He links this to Revelation 22:18–19. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
Ellicott notes the text says "the word," not "the words." He takes "the word" to mean the core of the Law, and says the Law of Moses holds the seed of all later revelation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Clarke takes it strictly: don't add any book, chapter, verse or word that God didn't speak. Matthew Henry gives two older readings. One is about practice: don't add sins or leave out duties. The other is about belief: don't add your own inventions or extra rites of worship. Coffman, quoting Craigie, says the church has historically applied this verse, with Revelation 22:18–19, to the canon of Scripture. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-2.html)
Question: if nothing may be added, how could more Scripture come later? Bible Hub's answer: the command does not forbid further messages from the same divine Source. Rather, it prevents any unauthorized interference with what God has declared. (https://biblehub.com/q/how_reconcile_deut._4_2_with_later_changes.htm)

**v. 3:** Guzik: at Baal-peor Israel fell into both sexual and spiritual sin with the women of Moab and Midian (Numbers 25). Thousands died, only months before Moses gave this speech. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
Ellicott: the Hebrew means "your eyes are the ones that see," so the listeners were themselves witnesses. He thinks the 24,000 who died were all from the younger generation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

**vv. 3–4:** Guzik: Moses tells the survivors of that judgment to keep on being faithful. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 5:** Ellicott stresses that Moses' law is tied to the land of Canaan. Many of its commands could only be kept by a chosen people living in a protected land. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

**v. 6:** Guzik: God meant an obedient, thriving Israel to be a witness that other nations would notice. His example is the queen of Sheba visiting Solomon (1 Kings 10). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 7:** Guzik: by size or population Israel wasn't a great nation. It would become great by keeping the covenant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
Matthew Henry: Those who call upon God, shall certainly find him within call, ready to give an answer of peace to every prayer of faith. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)

**v. 8:** Ellicott sees the Law as well ahead of its own time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Guzik adds that God entrusted his word to Israel (Romans 3:2), a gift to all people. He quotes Clarke: much of what is best in Asian and European law was borrowed from Moses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 9:** Guzik: Israel's faith rests on things that really happened, not on myths or speculation. The New Testament does the same, resting on Christ's death and resurrection. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
Ellicott: Israel failed to teach its children (Judges 2:10). He also notes that when teaching is left only to parents, it is often neglected. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

**v. 10:** Ellicott: the Greek Old Testament's word for "gather" is related to *ekklesia* (church). It could be paraphrased "form a Church of this people." It may lie behind Stephen's phrase "the church in the wilderness" (Acts 7:38). He compares Sinai, about fifty days after Passover, with Pentecost. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Guzik, quoting Thompson, calls the fear of the Lord the proper human response to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 11:** Ellicott links the darkness and cloud to the "blackness, and darkness, and tempest" of Hebrews 12:18. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

**v. 12:** Matthew Henry: God spoke in words, not in a visible shape, to teach that faith comes by hearing. Seeing God as he is is saved for the next world. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-15.html)

**v. 13:** Guzik, quoting Merrill: the two tablets were probably duplicate copies, each with all ten commandments, one for each party to the covenant. Also via Merrill: this is the first time Deuteronomy uses *berit* (covenant). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**vv. 15–16:** Ellicott: idolatry corrupts in two ways. It turns the glory of God into an image of a creature, and it ends up corrupting the worshipper. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Matthew Henry: There may be idols in the heart, where there are none in the sanctuary. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-15.html)
Keil & Delitzsch: what is banned here is making an image of the LORD in order to worship him through it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-15.htm)

**vv. 16–19:** Barnes reads these verses as a complete list of the idolatries around Israel:
- human-shaped household and city gods (v. 16)
- Egypt's animal worship (vv. 17–18)
- worship of the sun, moon and stars (v. 19)

(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-15.htm)

**v. 19:** Barnes: the heavenly bodies were "divided" to the nations for their use and benefit. Since they serve people, they must not be worshipped as lords. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)
Ellicott: the stars belong to every nation and protect none in particular, but the LORD bound himself to be Israel's God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Translations differ on this verse. The Douay-Rheims says God *created* them for the service of all the nations. The CEV says The LORD put them there for all the other nations to worship. (https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/4-19.htm)

**v. 20:** Guzik: because God rescued Israel, he has a claim on their loyalty. All people owe God honour as Creator; his people also owe it to him as Redeemer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
JFB: an iron-smelting furnace is the hottest picture available for Israel's slavery. Leaving God for Egypt's idols would be the worst ingratitude. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)
Bible.org: a furnace turns unusable ore into usable metal, and that is a picture of what God did with Israel in Egypt. (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-4)

**vv. 21–22:** Guzik: God disciplined Moses for Israel's sake, to show that no one is above God's law. Moses accepted that he could be replaced: God's workers come and go, but his work goes on. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
Ellicott sums up Moses' point as "I can't go with you to warn you, so take more care on your own." He compares Paul's last charge to Timothy. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)
Keil & Delitzsch: Numbers 20 doesn't mention God swearing an oath, but that doesn't make the oath doubtful. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)

**v. 23:** Guzik: taking the land depended less on Joshua's leadership than on Israel keeping the covenant and refusing idols. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**v. 24:** Guzik puts Moses' logic this way: if God didn't spare me when I sinned, don't think he will spare you if you turn to other gods. Quoting Thompson, he says *qanna* (jealous) means an active zeal for righteousness that comes from God's holiness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)
- Pulpit Commentary: the phrase echoes the fire seen on Sinai (Exodus 24:17). God is jealous for his glory and over his people, because he loves them.
- Benson and Poole: God is like a husband who won't tolerate rival lovers.
- Gill: God is a consuming fire to his enemies, especially idolaters.
- Ellicott: Hebrews 12:29 applies the verse to Pentecost and to the voice that speaks from heaven. (Bible Hub prints the reference as "Deuteronomy 12:29," which is clearly a typo for Hebrews.)

(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)
NET note: putting "fire" next to "jealous" fits Deuteronomy 6:15. God's jealousy is not petty envy but response to an act of insubordination that must be severely judged. (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Deu&chapter=4&verse=24)
Bible.org: "jealous" points to God's loving, marriage-like commitment to Israel (Hosea 1–3). (https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-4)

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 15–16: Are pictures of Christ allowed?** This is the clearest split.
- **Lutheran:** Chad Bird (1517) says Lutherans may freely use icons, crucifixes and paintings of Christ, while Many traditional Reformed communions teach otherwise. His reason: at Sinai God showed no form, but in the incarnation he made himself visible and touchable. (https://www.1517.org/articles/are-images-of-jesus-a-violation-of-the-commandments)
- **Strict Reformed (TGC):** one article reads Deuteronomy 4:15–24 as a commentary on the second commandment. Since Christ is God, images of Christ are forbidden too. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/images-christ-no/)
- **Puritan:** Thomas Watson argues that picturing Christ's humanity without his Godhead makes him "but half Christ." (https://biblehub.com/library/watson/the_ten_commandments/2_2_the_second_commandment.htm)
- **Reformed but more moderate (Ligonier):** what's forbidden is an image of the divine nature, and this does not rule out images of Jesus. (https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/the-second-commandment/) Another Ligonier piece notes that Westminster-style Puritan thought bans pictures in the sanctuary, while continental Reformed churches have allowed art; Ligonier sides with the continental view. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/images-worship)
- **TGC (Justin Taylor):** posts a pro-image argument that contrasts "no form" at Sinai with the visible Christ of 1 John 1. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/arguments-for-and-against-images-of-the-incarnate-christ/)
- **Calvary Chapel-style teaching:** Chuck Smith says he personally dislikes pictures of Christ but doesn't bind others on it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-15.html)

**v. 2: Scripture and tradition.** John MacArthur (GTY, Baptist-leaning) uses the verse to show that God's written word was the final authority and was not to be supplemented by any other authority. He sees this as a case against raising tradition to Scripture's level, as in Judaism and Rome. (https://www.gty.org/articles/A244/scripture-tradition-and-rome-part-1)

## 3. Other views

**Catholic, v. 2:** Catholic Answers replies that the Deuteronomy texts are about Israel keeping the Mosaic Law, so These passages do not prove what is claimed against Tradition and the Magisterium. (https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/adding-to-scripture)

**Catholic, vv. 15–18:** Early Israel was barred from picturing God because he hadn't shown himself in visible form, and because pagan surroundings made idolatry tempting. In Christ, though, God showed an "icon" of himself (Colossians 1:15). (https://www.catholic.com/tract/do-catholics-worship-statues)
Tim Staples argues that because the Law itself commanded cherubim and the bronze serpent, the ban was on images *of God*. The incarnation opens a "new economy" of images. (https://www.catholic.com/video/i-m-not-catholic-because-of-your-statues)

**Modern scholarship:**
- Von Rad, cited by Coffman, says the "do not add or take away" formula is very old in the ancient Near East. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-2.html)
- Craigie, cited by Coffman, says limiting God, whether by material form or theological proposition, fails to respect how far beyond us he is. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-15.html)
- The Cambridge Bible notes that "devouring fire" is common in Isaiah, and makes a source-critical remark on the singular/plural wording of v. 24. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-24.htm)
